questions.q: Which feature is the hallmark of delirium, without which the diagnosis should be questioned?
ch: Depressed mood with anhedonia lasting at least two weeks
Progressive memory loss developing gradually over months to years
Fixed persecutory delusions with a preserved level of consciousness
Inattention with an acute, fluctuating course
Tremor and autonomic instability with a normal attention span
questions.exp: Inattention is the hallmark of delirium — acute onset with a fluctuating course plus inattention forms the core of the CAM. If attention is intact, question the diagnosis.
why: Depressed mood with anhedonia suggests depression, a key differential that hypoactive delirium is frequently mistaken for.
Gradual progressive memory loss over months to years describes dementia, which is chronic and spares attention early.
Fixed delusions with a clear sensorium describe a psychotic disorder; delirium disturbs attention and awareness and fluctuates.
Tremor and autonomic instability point to alcohol or sedative withdrawal as a precipitant rather than defining delirium itself.

questions.q: Which delirium subtype is the most common and the most frequently missed?
ch: Hypoactive — lethargic and withdrawn, mistaken for depression or fatigue
Hyperactive — agitated and hallucinating, easily recognized at the bedside
Mixed — alternating agitation and lethargy across a single hospital day
Nocturnal — confusion confined entirely to the overnight hours
Catatonic — mutism and posturing with no fluctuation in awareness
questions.exp: Hypoactive delirium, in which the patient is lethargic and withdrawn, is the most common subtype and the most missed because it is mistaken for depression or fatigue; it also carries worse mortality.
why: Hyperactive delirium with agitation and hallucinations is the subtype that gets recognized, not the one that is missed.
Mixed delirium is a recognized subtype, but hypoactive is named as the most common and most missed.
Sundowning describes worsening at night, but a nocturnal subtype is not one of the three listed.
Catatonia is not one of the three subtypes described (hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed).

questions.q: Using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), which combination of features establishes delirium?
ch: Acute and fluctuating course AND inattention, PLUS disorganized thinking OR altered consciousness
Acute and fluctuating course plus disorganized thinking, with attention fully preserved
Inattention plus an altered level of consciousness, with gradual onset over several weeks
Any two of the four CAM features, in any combination at all
Disorganized thinking plus altered consciousness, regardless of attention
questions.exp: The CAM requires feature 1 (acute onset and fluctuating course) AND feature 2 (inattention), plus either feature 3 (disorganized thinking) or feature 4 (altered level of consciousness).
why: Inattention is mandatory; a case with preserved attention does not meet CAM and should prompt reconsideration.
Onset must be acute with a fluctuating course — a gradual course over weeks points toward dementia.
The CAM is not any-two-of-four; features 1 and 2 are both required before a third feature counts.
These are features 3 and 4, but neither substitutes for the required inattention.

questions.q: In which situation is a benzodiazepine the appropriate treatment for a delirious patient?
ch: Hypoactive delirium with a disrupted sleep-wake cycle
Agitated delirium in a mechanically ventilated ICU patient
Delirium superimposed on dementia in a frail elderly patient
Any severe agitation that has not responded to a first dose of haloperidol
Delirium caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal
questions.exp: Benzodiazepines otherwise worsen and precipitate delirium; the one exception is alcohol or sedative withdrawal delirium and withdrawal seizures, where lorazepam is indicated.
why: Melatonin or ramelteon restores the sleep-wake cycle; a sedative adds burden and worsens delirium.
In the ICU, dexmedetomidine is preferred over benzodiazepines, which cause more delirium.
Elderly patients with dementia are the most vulnerable to benzodiazepine-precipitated delirium, not an exception.
Benzodiazepines are not the escalation step for refractory agitation — they worsen and precipitate delirium.

questions.q: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized older adult with new fluctuating confusion. Which intervention is first-line for both prevention and treatment?
ch: Nightly lorazepam to consolidate sleep and reduce nighttime wandering
A non-pharmacologic bundle: reorientation, sleep hygiene, mobility, and sensory aids
Quetiapine at bedtime for sleep disturbance and mild agitation
Scheduled low-dose haloperidol around the clock every eight hours
Soft wrist restraints applied routinely to keep lines and catheters in place
questions.exp: The non-pharmacologic bundle — reorientation, sleep hygiene, mobility, glasses and hearing aids — is first-line for prevention and treatment, is superior to any drug, and is the basis of the HELP program and the ABCDEF bundle.
why: Benzodiazepines worsen and precipitate delirium outside of alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
Quetiapine may help agitation with sleep disturbance, but antipsychotics are not first-line and carry a black box warning in elderly dementia.
Haloperidol is reserved for severe agitation that endangers the patient or others and has not been shown to shorten delirium.
Restraints worsen agitation and are a last resort; tethers such as lines and catheters should be removed when possible.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter imbalance explains why anticholinergic drugs precipitate delirium?
ch: Glutamate depletion from reduced NMDA receptor signaling
Relative cholinergic deficiency with dopaminergic excess
Cholinergic excess with depletion of central dopamine
Serotonin excess from impaired reuptake in the brainstem
GABA deficiency that is corrected by benzodiazepine therapy
questions.exp: Delirium reflects global cerebral dysfunction with relative cholinergic deficiency and dopamine excess, which explains why anticholinergics precipitate it and why antipsychotics can control the agitation.
why: Reduced glutamate signaling is not the imbalance described; acetylcholine and dopamine are.
This reverses the described imbalance; cholinergic excess would not be worsened by anticholinergic drugs.
Serotonin excess is not the mechanism given for delirium.
GABA deficiency would imply benzodiazepines help, yet benzodiazepines cause delirium outside withdrawal.

questions.q: An anticoagulated patient develops acute confusion after an unwitnessed fall and now has a new focal neurologic deficit. What is the priority action?
ch: Start scheduled haloperidol for symptomatic agitation control
Obtain an EEG to exclude nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Obtain urgent neuroimaging to exclude stroke or hemorrhage
Begin a lorazepam taper for presumed sedative withdrawal
Apply the reorientation bundle and reassess in the morning
questions.exp: A new focal neurologic deficit, seizure, or head trauma — especially with anticoagulation — is a red flag requiring urgent CT or MRI to exclude stroke or hemorrhage.
why: Antipsychotics treat agitation symptomatically and would delay identifying a structural cause.
EEG is reserved for suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus; trauma with a focal deficit demands imaging first.
Nothing here suggests alcohol or sedative withdrawal, and benzodiazepines otherwise worsen delirium.
The non-pharmacologic bundle is essential care but does not address a possible intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.q: For an agitated, mechanically ventilated ICU patient, which sedation strategy reduces delirium duration?
ch: Continuous midazolam infusion titrated to deep sedation
Intermittent lorazepam boluses given as needed for agitation
Scheduled diphenhydramine every night for sleep
A high-dose opioid infusion used as the sole sedative
Dexmedetomidine, with monitoring for bradycardia and hypotension
questions.exp: Dexmedetomidine causes less delirium than benzodiazepines and is preferred for sedation in ventilated agitated ICU patients under the ABCDEF bundle; it requires ICU monitoring because it causes bradycardia and hypotension.
why: A benzodiazepine infusion is exactly what the ABCDEF and PADIS approach avoids, because it increases delirium.
Lorazepam is reserved for alcohol or sedative withdrawal; otherwise benzodiazepines precipitate delirium.
Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic, and anticholinergics are a classic precipitant of delirium.
Opioids are among the drugs listed as precipitating delirium, not a strategy that reduces it.

questions.q: A patient with known dementia becomes abruptly inattentive and drowsy over 24 hours. Which statement is correct?
ch: Delirium cannot be diagnosed once dementia has been established
An abrupt change like this is diagnostic of dementia rather than delirium
This is the expected progression of dementia and needs no further workup
This is delirium superimposed on dementia and requires a hunt for a precipitant
Attention is impaired early in dementia, so this is simply a bad day
questions.exp: Acute onset with fluctuation and inattention is delirium, while dementia is chronic and progressive with attention preserved early; the two coexist as delirium superimposed on dementia, and the abrupt change demands a search for the underlying insult.
why: Delirium can and often does occur on top of dementia — that is the superimposed presentation.
An abrupt, fluctuating course is delirium; dementia is the chronic, gradual process.
Dementia progresses over months to years; an abrupt 24-hour change is delirium until proven otherwise.
Attention is preserved early in dementia, so new inattention signals delirium.

questions.q: Which statement about antipsychotics in delirium reflects the current evidence?
ch: Haloperidol is the preferred agent in Parkinson and Lewy body disease
They are first-line for hypoactive delirium in order to improve alertness
They carry a black box warning for increased mortality in elderly dementia and have not been shown to shorten delirium
Atypical agents are free of QTc prolongation and metabolic side effects
They shorten the duration of delirium and should be started at diagnosis
questions.exp: Antipsychotics have not been shown to shorten delirium and carry a black box warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia; reserve them, at the lowest dose for the shortest time, for dangerous agitation.
why: Haloperidol should be avoided in Parkinson and Lewy body disease; an atypical is preferred with parkinsonism.
Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation, not used to stimulate hypoactive patients.
Atypicals still require monitoring for QTc prolongation and metabolic effects.
They have not been shown to shorten delirium — correcting the precipitant is what resolves it.

questions.q: What does the evidence say about directly asking a patient whether they are thinking of suicide?
ch: It is only appropriate once the patient has already made an attempt
It is acceptable only if the patient raises the topic themselves first
It plants the idea and increases risk, so a written screening tool should be used instead
Asking does not increase risk and is protective; ask directly and non-judgmentally
It should be deferred until a psychiatrist is available to conduct the interview
questions.exp: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea — it is protective, and this is the single most-tested myth to bust. Ask directly and non-judgmentally about ideation, plan, intent, means, and preparatory acts.
why: Screening precedes an attempt — the whole point is to intervene before intent becomes action.
Patients frequently will not raise it, and direct non-judgmental questioning is what uncovers ideation.
Asking does not plant the idea; that belief is the myth this topic singles out for correction.
Any clinician should screen directly; waiting for psychiatry delays identifying an acute plan and access to means.

questions.q: Which factor is the single strongest predictor of a future suicide attempt?
ch: A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder
Living alone in an urban setting
A prior suicide attempt
Non-suicidal self-injury without intent to die
Female sex
questions.exp: A prior attempt is the single strongest predictor of a future attempt; other high-weight factors include firearm access, male sex, older age, hopelessness, command hallucinations, and recent discharge from psychiatric care.
why: Depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, substance use, and borderline personality disorder all drive risk, but no diagnosis outweighs a prior attempt.
Lacking social support raises risk and appears in the SAD PERSONS mnemonic, but it is not the strongest single predictor.
Non-suicidal self-injury is self-harm to regulate emotion without intent to die and is managed differently.
Male sex carries higher completion; female sex is not the strongest predictor of a future attempt.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the continuum of suicidal behavior?
ch: Attempt, preparatory acts, intent, plan, then active ideation
Passive ideation, active ideation, plan, intent, preparatory acts, attempt
Non-suicidal self-injury, passive ideation, attempt, then active ideation
Plan, passive ideation, intent, active ideation, then attempt
Hopelessness, command hallucinations, passive ideation, then plan
questions.exp: Suicidal behavior spans a continuum from passive ideation to active ideation, then plan, intent, preparatory acts, and attempt; assessment probes where the patient sits on this spectrum and how fixed that position is.
why: This reverses the sequence; an attempt is the endpoint rather than the starting point.
Non-suicidal self-injury is a separate entity with no intent to die and is not a stage on this continuum.
A plan follows active ideation rather than preceding passive ideation.
Hopelessness and command hallucinations are risk factors and warning signs, not stages of the continuum.

questions.q: Which statement about structured tools such as the C-SSRS, SAD PERSONS, and PHQ-9 is accurate?
ch: A low C-SSRS score reliably guarantees that the patient will remain safe
They replace clinical judgment and determine disposition entirely on their own
SAD PERSONS is the tool used to characterize the lethality of a specific plan
A positive PHQ-9 item 9 is by itself diagnostic of active suicidal intent
They standardize assessment and documentation but do not replace clinical judgment
questions.exp: Structured tools such as the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, SAD PERSONS, and PHQ-9 standardize assessment and documentation, but they aid rather than replace clinical judgment, and risk is dynamic so reassessment at transitions of care is essential.
why: Risk is dynamic and fluctuating, so a low-risk assessment does not guarantee future safety.
These tools aid documentation and consistency but explicitly do not replace clinical judgment.
The C-SSRS is the instrument used to characterize ideation and lethality; SAD PERSONS is a risk-factor mnemonic.
PHQ-9 item 9 is a screen that prompts a fuller assessment, not a diagnosis of intent.

questions.q: Which two agents have the strongest evidence for reducing suicide, and in which populations?
ch: Lithium in bipolar and recurrent unipolar depression, and clozapine in schizophrenia
Valproate in bipolar disorder and haloperidol in schizoaffective disorder
Buspirone in anxiety disorders and naltrexone in alcohol use disorder
Sertraline in adolescents and quetiapine in schizophrenia
Ketamine in bipolar disorder and ECT in borderline personality disorder
questions.exp: Lithium has robust anti-suicide evidence in bipolar and recurrent unipolar depression and reduces all-cause mortality, and clozapine is FDA-approved to reduce suicidal behavior in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder.
why: Neither valproate nor haloperidol is named among the agents that reduce suicide.
Neither agent reduces suicide; treating a substance use disorder addresses a risk factor only.
SSRIs treat the underlying depression but carry a black-box warning for increased suicidality under 25, and quetiapine has no anti-suicide indication.
Ketamine and ECT act rapidly on acute suicidality but are not the agents with durable anti-suicide evidence.

questions.q: A patient with recent suicidal ideation is preparing for discharge. Which intervention is evidence-based?
ch: Reassurance that risk is lowest in the days right after discharge
A signed no-suicide contract placed in the chart before discharge
A collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, and 988
A promise from the nurse to keep the ideation secret from the family
Deferring any follow-up appointment until the patient requests one
questions.exp: A collaboratively built safety plan — warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline — is the evidence-based intervention; the no-suicide contract is not protective, and the post-discharge period is the highest-risk window.
why: The post-discharge period is the highest-risk window, not the lowest.
A no-suicide contract is not evidence-based and provides no protection.
Never promise to keep ideation secret; counseling the family on lethal-means storage requires involving them.
Close post-discharge follow-up and caring contacts reduce reattempt in the highest-risk window.

questions.q: A severely depressed inpatient who was withdrawn and psychomotor-retarded now appears brighter and more energetic. Why does the nurse increase vigilance?
ch: Risk rises as psychomotor retardation lifts, giving the patient the volition to act before mood recovers
Recovery of speech and engagement rules out ongoing suicidal ideation
Improvement in mood confirms the antidepressant has reached full effect
Increased energy means the patient can safely be moved off observation
Brightening always means the SSRI dose should be immediately reduced
questions.exp: Risk rises in the improving-depression window: psychomotor retardation lifts before mood recovers, so the patient regains the energy and volition to act. A sudden calm in a previously distraught patient may signal a resolved decision to die.
why: Improved speech does not exclude ideation, and sudden calm may reflect a resolved decision to die.
SSRIs may take weeks to work, and early improvement is when monitoring must be closest rather than relaxed.
This is precisely when the ordered level of observation should be maintained, because regained energy enables action.
Dose reduction is not indicated and would not address the acute risk window.

questions.q: A patient swallowed six acetaminophen tablets believing the dose would be fatal. How should this be interpreted?
ch: Risk is determined solely by whether the patient left a written note
High risk — perceived lethality with high intent matters more than the objective lethality of the act
Low risk — the objective lethality of the dose was minimal, so this was only a gesture
Low risk — this is non-suicidal self-injury, since the dose taken could not kill
Risk cannot be assessed at all until the acetaminophen level returns from the lab
questions.exp: A low-lethality act carried out with high intent — the patient believed it would kill them — is high risk; use the patient's perceived lethality, not just objective lethality. Acetaminophen and salicylate levels are still drawn as part of medical stabilization.
why: A note is one preparatory act among several and is not required for the risk to be high.
Objective lethality alone understates risk; the belief that the act would be fatal defines high intent.
Non-suicidal self-injury is self-harm to regulate emotion with no intent to die, and intent to die was present here.
Acetaminophen and salicylate levels are part of medical stabilization, but risk stratification does not wait on them.

questions.q: Which presentation most clearly warrants inpatient admission, including an involuntary hold if necessary?
ch: An attempt ten years ago in a patient who is currently euthymic and future-oriented
Chronic non-suicidal self-injury with no intent to die and an established therapist
Hopelessness alone with no ideation, no plan, and no access to lethal means
Active ideation with a specific plan, intent, and a firearm at home
Passive ideation without a plan, strong social support, and engagement in outpatient therapy
questions.exp: Active ideation with a specific plan, intent, and access to lethal means — especially firearms — is a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate one-to-one safety and likely admission, voluntary or involuntary.
why: A remote attempt raises static risk, but a euthymic, future-oriented patient with no current ideation does not need admission.
Non-suicidal self-injury without intent to die is managed differently and does not by itself require a hold.
Hopelessness is a high-weight risk factor, but with no ideation, plan, or means the acuity does not meet criteria for a hold.
Passive ideation with protective factors and a therapeutic alliance can be managed with intensive outpatient care and a safety plan.

questions.q: Which option is the fastest and most effective treatment for acutely suicidal, catatonic, or psychotic depression?
ch: Switching the patient from lithium to valproate
A standing dose of lorazepam for agitation
Starting an SSRI and waiting for the therapeutic effect to appear
Adding buspirone to an existing antidepressant regimen
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
questions.exp: ECT is the fastest, most effective option for acutely suicidal, catatonic, or psychotic depression; consider it when a rapid response is life-saving, accepting transient memory effects and the need for an anesthesia workup.
why: Lithium is the agent with anti-suicide evidence, so switching away from it removes that protection.
Sedation does not treat the depression that is driving the suicidality.
SSRIs may take weeks to work and carry a black-box warning for increased suicidality under 25 — far too slow here.
Buspirone is not among the treatments named for acute suicidality.

questions.q: Which finding set defines preeclampsia?
ch: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the third trimester with a normal blood pressure
Hypertension present before 20 weeks with proteinuria of at least 300 mg per 24 hours
New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks that always requires proteinuria for diagnosis
Isolated proteinuria after 20 weeks with normal blood pressure throughout pregnancy
New-onset blood pressure at or above 140/90 after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
questions.exp: Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension (at or above 140/90) after 20 weeks gestation plus either proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; proteinuria is no longer required when end-organ features are present.
why: A seizure in a preeclamptic patient is eclampsia, which arises from preeclampsia rather than defining it.
Hypertension predating 20 weeks is chronic hypertension, a risk factor rather than preeclampsia itself.
Proteinuria is no longer required — end-organ dysfunction alone establishes the diagnosis.
Hypertension is required; isolated proteinuria with normal pressures does not meet the criteria.

questions.q: What is the role of magnesium sulfate in severe preeclampsia?
ch: It replaces delivery as definitive treatment once severe features appear
It is the first-line agent for lowering severe-range blood pressure
It is given for seizure prophylaxis and for treating recurrent eclamptic seizures
It accelerates fetal lung maturity when delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks
It reverses the anti-angiogenic imbalance driving endothelial dysfunction
questions.exp: Magnesium sulfate is first-line for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and for treating and preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures; its benefit is anticonvulsant and neuroprotective, not antihypertensive.
why: Delivery remains the only cure, and magnesium is a temporizing measure.
Labetalol, hydralazine, and nifedipine lower blood pressure — magnesium is not an antihypertensive.
Betamethasone is the antenatal corticosteroid given for fetal lung maturity before 34 weeks.
Nothing reverses the sFlt-1/PlGF imbalance; delivery of the placenta is the only cure.

questions.q: Which finding qualifies as a severe feature of preeclampsia?
ch: Dipstick proteinuria of 2+ on a clean-catch urine specimen
Blood pressure of 148/94 confirmed on readings four hours apart
Mild dependent lower-extremity edema noted at 34 weeks gestation
A uric acid level at the upper limit of the reference range
Platelet count below 100,000 with new visual scotomata
questions.exp: Severe features include blood pressure at or above 160/110, platelets below 100k, creatinine above 1.1 or doubled, AST/ALT at least twice normal, pulmonary edema, and new cerebral or visual symptoms such as headache or scotomata.
why: Dipstick 2+ satisfies the proteinuria criterion but is not itself a severe feature.
Severe-range hypertension begins at 160/110; 148/94 meets the diagnostic threshold without severe features.
Edema reflects capillary leak but is not part of the severe-feature list.
Uric acid is drawn as part of the workup but is not a severe-feature criterion.

questions.q: What is the only definitive treatment for preeclampsia?
ch: Delivery of the placenta
Intravenous magnesium sulfate continued until the blood pressure normalizes
Maximal antihypertensive therapy with labetalol and nifedipine together
Low-dose aspirin started immediately at the time of diagnosis
Bed rest in the left lateral position until 37 weeks gestation
questions.exp: Delivery is the only cure, and it is delivery of the placenta rather than the fetus alone that ends the disease; everything else is temporizing while gestational age is balanced against maternal risk.
why: Magnesium prevents seizures but does not cure the underlying placental disease.
Antihypertensives protect the mother from stroke but do not treat the syndrome itself.
Aspirin is preventive, started at 12 to 28 weeks in high-risk patients, and is not a treatment once disease is established.
Positioning and monitoring are supportive measures only.

questions.q: A patient receiving a magnesium sulfate infusion has lost her patellar reflexes. What does this indicate, and what should be at the bedside?
ch: A normal finding in pregnancy; document it and continue routine monitoring
Therapeutic effect; continue the infusion at the current rate
Impending eclampsia; increase the magnesium infusion rate
Early magnesium toxicity; calcium gluconate should be at the bedside
Hypocalcemia; give oral calcium supplementation with the next meal
questions.exp: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity, which progresses to respiratory depression and then cardiac arrest; the antidote is IV calcium gluconate, kept at the bedside during the infusion.
why: Reflexes are assessed hourly precisely because their loss is abnormal and signals toxicity.
Absent reflexes are not the therapeutic endpoint — they are the first warning of toxicity.
Increasing the rate would deepen the toxicity that absent reflexes already signal.
Calcium gluconate is given intravenously as the antidote for magnesium toxicity, not orally for hypocalcemia.

questions.q: A woman at 33 weeks reports right upper quadrant pain and malaise; her blood pressure is 138/86. What does this presentation demand?
ch: No further testing, since the blood pressure is below the diagnostic threshold
A repeat blood pressure in one week at the next scheduled prenatal visit
Immediate delivery without any laboratory evaluation beforehand
LFTs, platelets, and LDH to evaluate for HELLP syndrome
MRI of the brain to exclude posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
questions.exp: HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) can present with normal or only mildly elevated blood pressure and minimal proteinuria, so order LFTs, platelets, and LDH for right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, and watch for subcapsular hepatic hematoma.
why: HELLP can occur with normal or only mildly elevated pressures, so a sub-threshold reading does not exclude it.
Deferring evaluation for a week risks hepatic rupture and rapid decompensation.
Delivery is the cure, but severity must first be established with laboratory evaluation.
Imaging for PRES is reserved for atypical or focal neurologic presentations, not right upper quadrant pain.

questions.q: A woman presents five days after an uncomplicated delivery with a new severe headache. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
ch: A tension headache from sleep deprivation with a newborn at home
Postpartum preeclampsia
Migraine recurrence now that the pregnancy has ended
Dehydration related to breastfeeding and poor oral intake
Post-dural-puncture headache from her labor analgesia
questions.exp: Preeclampsia can present or worsen up to 6 weeks postpartum, so a new severe postpartum headache is preeclampsia until proven otherwise; magnesium is continued at least 24 hours postpartum with ongoing blood pressure surveillance.
why: Attributing a new severe postpartum headache to fatigue risks missing eclampsia and maternal stroke.
Assuming migraine delays the blood pressure check and laboratory workup this presentation requires.
Dehydration does not explain a new severe headache in the postpartum window.
A positional headache after neuraxial anesthesia is possible, but preeclampsia must be excluded first.

questions.q: Which mechanism underlies the maternal endothelial dysfunction of preeclampsia?
ch: Shallow trophoblast invasion causing placental ischemia with a rise in sFlt-1 and a fall in PlGF
Excess placental lactogen production causing maternal insulin resistance
Autoimmune destruction of the maternal glomerular basement membrane
Platelet consumption caused by a deficiency of ADAMTS13
Direct fetal antibody-mediated injury to maternal blood vessels
questions.exp: Poor trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries produces placental hypoperfusion and release of anti-angiogenic factors — sFlt-1 rises and sequesters VEGF and PlGF — causing systemic endothelial dysfunction, vasospasm, and capillary leak.
why: Placental lactogen drives insulin resistance in gestational diabetes, not preeclamptic endothelial injury.
Preeclampsia is not an autoimmune glomerular disease, although autoimmune disease raises the risk.
ADAMTS13 deficiency describes TTP, which sits in the differential but is not the mechanism here.
There is no fetal antibody-mediated attack on maternal vessels in this syndrome.

questions.q: For a patient at high risk of preeclampsia, when should low-dose aspirin be started?
ch: In the third trimester, once fetal growth restriction appears
Immediately postpartum, to prevent recurrence in a later pregnancy
Between 12 and 28 weeks, ideally before 16 weeks
Only once proteinuria has been documented on a prenatal visit
At the first appearance of a severe-range blood pressure reading
questions.exp: Low-dose aspirin 81 mg is preventive in high-risk patients and is started at 12 to 28 weeks, ideally before 16 weeks; it reduces preeclampsia risk but is not a treatment once disease is established.
why: Starting in the third trimester is too late; the benefit depends on early initiation.
Postpartum initiation does nothing for the disease already present in this pregnancy.
Aspirin is prevention, not treatment — once proteinuria appears the window has passed.
Severe-range blood pressure calls for labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine, not aspirin.

questions.q: How does the presence of severe features change delivery timing in preeclampsia?
ch: Delivery timing is identical whether or not severe features are present
Without severe features deliver at 37 weeks or later; with severe features expedite, often at 34 weeks or immediately
With severe features, delivery is postponed until betamethasone can be given at 36 weeks
Delivery is indicated only after an eclamptic seizure has actually occurred
Delivery is delayed to 40 weeks in both groups to maximize fetal maturity
questions.exp: Delivery timing is framed around with versus without severe features: deliver at 37 weeks or later without severe features, and expedite delivery — often at 34 weeks or immediately — with severe features or maternal instability.
why: The with-versus-without severe features distinction is exactly what dictates timing.
Betamethasone is given when time permits and must never delay urgent delivery.
Waiting for a seizure means waiting for eclampsia, which magnesium prophylaxis and timely delivery exist to prevent.
Neither group is carried to 40 weeks; expectant management trades fetal maturity against maternal risk.

questions.q: Which hormone is the main driver of pregnancy-related insulin resistance?
ch: Fetal insulin crossing the placenta into the maternal circulation
Maternal thyroid-stimulating hormone rising in the first trimester
Oxytocin released progressively across the third trimester
Prolactin suppressing maternal hepatic gluconeogenesis
Human placental lactogen (hPL)
questions.exp: hPL is the main driver of pregnancy insulin resistance and its diabetogenic effect peaks in the third trimester; progesterone, cortisol, and growth hormone contribute, and GDM appears when maternal beta-cell output cannot compensate.
why: Fetal insulin does not cross into the mother; maternal glucose crosses to the fetus and drives fetal hyperinsulinemia.
TSH is not among the counter-regulatory hormones described as driving gestational insulin resistance.
Oxytocin has no role here; the drivers are hPL, progesterone, cortisol, and growth hormone.
Prolactin is not named as a driver, and the effect described is the opposite of insulin resistance.

questions.q: In the standard two-step U.S. approach, what is the first step of gestational diabetes screening at 24-28 weeks?
ch: A non-fasting 50 g glucose challenge with a one-hour draw
A fasting 100 g three-hour oral glucose tolerance test
Random capillary glucose checked at three consecutive visits
A fasting 75 g two-hour oral glucose tolerance test
A hemoglobin A1c drawn at the routine prenatal visit
questions.exp: Step 1 is the non-fasting 50 g glucose challenge test with a draw at 1 hour; a positive screen requires confirmation with the fasting 100 g 3-hour OGTT.
why: The 100 g 3-hour OGTT is the confirmatory second step, performed after a positive glucose challenge.
Random glucose checks are not the screening method used for gestational diabetes.
The fasting 75 g 2-hour OGTT is the one-step IADPSG/ADA alternative, not step 1 of the two-step pathway.
A1c is not the primary diagnostic test in pregnancy; an early elevated A1c instead indicates overt diabetes.

questions.q: Which set of self-monitoring blood glucose targets is used in gestational diabetes?
ch: Fasting under 110, 1-hour postprandial under 155, 2-hour under 140 mg/dL
Fasting under 120, 1-hour postprandial under 180, 2-hour under 160 mg/dL
Fasting under 95, 1-hour postprandial under 140, 2-hour under 120 mg/dL
Fasting under 70, 1-hour postprandial under 100, 2-hour under 90 mg/dL
Fasting under 130, 1-hour postprandial under 200, 2-hour under 180 mg/dL
questions.exp: Medical nutrition therapy with self-monitoring of blood glucose targets a fasting value under 95, a 1-hour postprandial under 140, and a 2-hour postprandial under 120 mg/dL; most patients reach control on diet alone as A1GDM.
why: These numbers mix the Carpenter-Coustan diagnostic values with treatment targets.
These thresholds are far too permissive and would allow sustained maternal hyperglycemia.
These targets sit below normal physiology and would risk maternal hypoglycemia.
These values approach the diagnostic thresholds themselves rather than treatment targets.

questions.q: Diet and exercise fail to control a patient's glucose at 30 weeks. What is the preferred pharmacotherapy, and why?
ch: A combination of metformin and a sulfonylurea for broader coverage
Insulin, because it does not cross the placenta
No pharmacotherapy; intensify the diet until delivery regardless of the readings
Glyburide, because an oral agent improves adherence
Metformin, because it is the ACOG and ADA drug of choice in pregnancy
questions.exp: Insulin is the preferred first-line pharmacotherapy for A2GDM and the ACOG/ADA drug of choice because it does not cross the placenta, whereas metformin and glyburide both do.
why: Combination oral therapy is not the recommended pathway; insulin is first-line once diet fails.
Failing diet therapy defines A2GDM and requires pharmacotherapy rather than further delay.
Glyburide crosses the placenta and carries higher rates of neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia than insulin.
Metformin is a reasonable alternative when insulin is declined, but it crosses the placenta and is not the drug of choice.

questions.q: What follow-up test is required after a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes?
ch: A 50 g glucose challenge on the day of hospital discharge
No testing, because gestational diabetes always resolves at delivery
Annual fasting insulin levels beginning at age fifty
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6-12 weeks postpartum
A hemoglobin A1c drawn at the six-month well-child visit
questions.exp: GDM usually resolves postpartum but raises later maternal type 2 diabetes risk by roughly 50%, so the 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum is always ordered to reclassify glucose status.
why: The glucose challenge is an antenatal screening tool; reclassification uses the 75 g OGTT weeks later.
It usually resolves, but the lifetime type 2 diabetes risk is exactly why reclassification is mandatory.
Waiting decades misses the substantially elevated near-term type 2 diabetes risk.
Reclassification testing is for the mother in the early postpartum window, not at a well-child visit.

questions.q: A macrosomic newborn of a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes becomes jittery an hour after birth. What explains this?
ch: Hypocalcemia is the only recognized cause of jitteriness in these infants
Delayed surfactant production directly lowers the neonatal glucose level
Placental lactogen keeps raising the newborn's insulin resistance after birth
Fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after cord clamping removes the maternal glucose supply
Maternal insulin crossed the placenta and still circulates in the neonate
questions.exp: Maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta and drives fetal hyperinsulinemia (the Pedersen hypothesis), causing macrosomia; once the cord is clamped the glucose supply stops while the hyperinsulinemia persists, producing neonatal hypoglycemia.
why: Hypocalcemia is part of the classic neonatal triad, but the jitteriness here is driven by hypoglycemia.
Delayed surfactant production causes respiratory distress rather than hypoglycemia.
Placental hormones stop acting on the newborn once the placenta has been delivered.
Insulin does not cross the placenta — that is precisely why insulin is the safe drug in pregnancy.

questions.q: Betamethasone is ordered at 31 weeks for a patient with insulin-treated gestational diabetes. What should be anticipated?
ch: An immediate need to switch from insulin therapy to oral metformin
Permanent conversion of A1GDM to lifelong insulin dependence after delivery
A sharp fall in maternal insulin requirements lasting about a week
No change in maternal glucose, since steroids act only on the fetal lung
A transient rise in maternal glucose for about 3-5 days, requiring insulin up-titration
questions.exp: Antenatal corticosteroids transiently raise maternal glucose for roughly 3-5 days; anticipate this and up-titrate insulin with closer monitoring rather than being caught out by the readings.
why: Insulin remains first-line, and metformin crosses the placenta and may not control steroid-driven hyperglycemia.
The hyperglycemic effect is transient, lasting only a few days rather than being permanent.
Steroids raise glucose rather than lowering it, so insulin requirements climb instead of falling.
Betamethasone has a well-described hyperglycemic effect on the mother.

questions.q: A patient's first prenatal visit at 9 weeks shows a hemoglobin A1c of 6.9%. How should this be interpreted?
ch: Evidence of laboratory error, since A1c cannot be measured during pregnancy
Gestational diabetes found early, managed identically to disease found at 26 weeks
Overt, pre-existing diabetes, carrying a higher risk of congenital malformations
A normal pregnancy value that requires no further evaluation
An indication to proceed to the routine 50 g glucose challenge at 28 weeks
questions.exp: An early A1c at or above 6.5% indicates overt, pre-existing (undiagnosed type 2) diabetes rather than true GDM; because organogenesis occurred in hyperglycemia, the risk of congenital malformations is higher.
why: A1c can be measured in pregnancy; it simply is not the primary diagnostic test for GDM.
Glucose intolerance identified in the first trimester is overt diabetes, not true gestational diabetes.
An A1c at this level is abnormal at any point in pregnancy and demands action.
Waiting for routine screening ignores an already-diagnostic value and delays management.

questions.q: Which delivery complication should be anticipated when gestational diabetes has produced macrosomia?
ch: Cord prolapse caused directly by fetal hyperinsulinemia
Shoulder dystocia, risking brachial plexus injury and asphyxia
Amniotic fluid embolism triggered by antenatal steroid administration
Uterine inversion caused by a rapid second stage of labor
Placenta previa developing during the course of labor
questions.exp: Macrosomia from fetal hyperinsulinemia raises the risk of shoulder dystocia, an obstetric emergency threatening brachial plexus injury and asphyxia — which is why adherence and antenatal growth surveillance matter.
why: Fetal hyperinsulinemia produces macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia, not cord prolapse.
Antenatal steroids raise maternal glucose; they do not cause amniotic fluid embolism.
Uterine inversion is not the complication linked to macrosomia in gestational diabetes.
Placenta previa is established earlier in pregnancy and is unrelated to fetal size.

questions.q: What distinguishes A1GDM from A2GDM?
ch: A1GDM is controlled with diet and exercise; A2GDM requires pharmacotherapy
A1GDM is diagnosed by the one-step test and A2GDM by the two-step test
A1GDM occurs in the first trimester and A2GDM only after 24 weeks
A1GDM carries no fetal risk, whereas A2GDM alone causes macrosomia
A1GDM resolves postpartum whereas A2GDM never resolves at all
questions.exp: A1GDM is diet- and exercise-controlled while A2GDM requires pharmacotherapy; roughly 70-85% of patients achieve control on diet alone, and the classification ties into delivery timing and the intensity of antenatal surveillance.
why: Either classification can follow either diagnostic pathway; the distinction is about treatment, not the test used.
First-trimester hyperglycemia indicates overt pre-existing diabetes, not A1GDM.
Both classes carry fetal risk, and macrosomia follows from hyperglycemia regardless of treatment.
GDM of either class usually resolves postpartum, which is why reclassification testing is ordered.

questions.q: Which of the 4 T's accounts for roughly 70-80% of postpartum hemorrhage?
ch: Tone — uterine atony
Trauma — lacerations, hematoma, or uterine rupture
Tissue — retained placenta or products of conception
Thrombin — coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Thrombosis — a deep venous clot embolizing during the third stage
questions.exp: Atony is the answer roughly 80% of the time: a boggy uterus with heavy bleeding calls for fundal massage and oxytocin before anything else, with trauma, tissue, and thrombin making up the remainder.
why: Trauma is one of the 4 T's, suspected when bleeding is brisk despite a firm fundus, but it is far less common than atony.
Retained tissue is a real cause, particularly in secondary PPH, but it is not the majority of cases.
Coagulopathy accounts for a small fraction and usually develops as a consequence of massive blood loss.
Thrombosis is not one of the 4 T's — the fourth T is thrombin.

questions.q: Which statement matches the updated ACOG definition of postpartum hemorrhage?
ch: A visually estimated loss exceeding two saturated pads in a single hour
Cumulative loss of 1000 mL or more, or any loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth regardless of route
Blood loss greater than 500 mL following a vaginal delivery only
Blood loss greater than 1500 mL following a cesarean delivery only
Any bleeding that requires a transfusion within the first postpartum week
questions.exp: The updated ACOG definition is cumulative blood loss of 1000 mL or more, or any blood loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth — and it applies regardless of delivery route.
why: Visual estimation is exactly what the definition moves away from in favor of quantitative blood loss.
The route-specific 500 mL threshold is the older definition; the current one is route-independent.
The current definition applies a single threshold to all delivery routes, not a higher one for cesarean.
Transfusion is not part of the definition, and the primary window is 24 hours rather than a week.

questions.q: A patient with preeclampsia has ongoing atony after oxytocin. Which uterotonic must be avoided?
ch: Oxytocin infusion, because a second dose is contraindicated
Carboprost, because it can trigger bronchospasm
Tranexamic acid, because of the risk of hypotension
Methylergonovine, because it is an ergot that raises blood pressure
Misoprostol, because it causes fever and shivering
questions.exp: Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia because it is an ergot that causes vasoconstriction and can spike the blood pressure; it is also given IM and never IV.
why: Oxytocin remains first-line and is given IM or as a diluted infusion rather than a rapid IV push.
Carboprost does cause bronchospasm, but that contraindication applies to asthma rather than preeclampsia.
TXA is an antifibrinolytic given within 3 hours of birth, and hypertension is not a contraindication to it.
Fever, shivering, and diarrhea are common misoprostol side effects, not a reason to withhold it here.

questions.q: A postpartum patient has heavy bleeding and a soft, boggy fundus displaced upward and to the right. What is the immediate nursing action?
ch: Prepare the patient for uterine artery embolization
Perform firm fundal massage and empty the bladder
Inspect the cervix and vagina for lacerations first
Send a fibrinogen level and wait for the result
Position the patient flat and restrict all oral intake
questions.exp: A boggy fundus displaced upward and to the right suggests atony with a full bladder; massage the fundus firmly and empty the bladder, because a distended bladder mechanically prevents contraction and is a fast, correctable cause of poor tone.
why: Embolization sits far down the escalation ladder, after massage, uterotonics, and balloon tamponade.
Inspection for trauma is indicated when bleeding continues with a firm fundus; this fundus is boggy.
Fibrinogen is drawn, but treatment cannot wait on a laboratory result in an actively bleeding patient.
Positioning and withholding oral intake do nothing to make the myometrium contract.

questions.q: A healthy 24-year-old has a heart rate of 118 and a blood pressure of 112/78 with ongoing bleeding after delivery. How should this be interpreted?
ch: Stable, since the blood pressure remains within normal limits
Expected postpartum tachycardia that requires no escalation
Evidence that the bleeding has stopped and compensation is complete
A rising shock index warning of hemorrhagic shock despite a normal blood pressure
An indication to hold uterotonics until hypotension actually develops
questions.exp: Young healthy mothers compensate, so tachycardia and a narrowing pulse pressure precede hypotension; a rising shock index (HR/SBP above 0.9-1.0) is an early warning, and the shock index and quantitative blood loss are more trustworthy than the blood pressure.
why: A normal blood pressure is falsely reassuring, because healthy young mothers compensate until they crash.
Tachycardia with active bleeding is an early sign of hypovolemia, not a finding to ignore.
Bleeding is described as ongoing, and compensation reflects loss rather than recovery.
Waiting for hypotension delays treatment well past the compensated phase.

questions.q: Within what window should tranexamic acid be given for postpartum hemorrhage?
ch: Only for secondary postpartum hemorrhage beyond 24 hours
At any point during the first postpartum week
Within 3 hours of birth
Within 12 hours of birth
Only after two units of packed red cells have been transfused
questions.exp: TXA is an antifibrinolytic given within 3 hours of birth; the WOMAN trial showed reduced death from bleeding, and the benefit falls off sharply after that window. It is an adjunct rather than a substitute for uterotonics or surgery.
why: The evidence and the treatment window concern bleeding within hours of birth.
Delaying to days after birth forfeits the benefit entirely.
The benefit falls off sharply after 3 hours, so a 12-hour window misses it.
TXA is given early alongside uterotonics rather than held until transfusion has begun.

questions.q: Why is a fibrinogen level of 190 mg/dL concerning in a bleeding postpartum patient?
ch: It falls in the normal non-pregnant range and is therefore reassuring
It indicates the patient has received too much tranexamic acid
It confirms retained placental tissue as the source of the bleeding
It effectively rules out disseminated intravascular coagulation
Fibrinogen is normally elevated in pregnancy, so a level under 200 predicts severe hemorrhage
questions.exp: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with an elevated baseline fibrinogen, so a normal-looking level below 200 mg/dL is actually low and predicts severe postpartum hemorrhage; replace fibrinogen early with cryoprecipitate.
why: The non-pregnant reference range is the wrong yardstick, because pregnancy raises the baseline level.
TXA is an antifibrinolytic and does not lower the fibrinogen level.
Retained tissue is identified by examination and uterine exploration, not by a fibrinogen level.
A falling fibrinogen with oozing from IV sites is exactly how developing DIC presents.

questions.q: Bleeding from atony continues despite massage, oxytocin, methylergonovine, and carboprost. What is the next step on the escalation ladder?
ch: Uterine balloon tamponade with a Bakri balloon
Observation with serial hemoglobin measurements
Discharge home on oral misoprostol with close follow-up
Proceed straight to hysterectomy as the first surgical option
Repeat the entire uterotonic sequence a second time
questions.exp: When medications fail, escalate to uterine balloon tamponade with a Bakri balloon, then uterine artery embolization, then surgical measures such as a B-Lynch compression suture or uterine artery ligation, with hysterectomy as definitive control.
why: Observation is unsafe with ongoing hemorrhage and refractory atony.
Discharging an actively bleeding mother is never appropriate.
Hysterectomy is definitive control at the end of the ladder, not the first surgical move.
Repeating agents that have already failed wastes time in an actively bleeding patient.

questions.q: A woman with a prior cesarean and known placenta previa has heavy bleeding and a placenta that will not separate. What should be suspected?
ch: Secondary postpartum hemorrhage caused by endometritis
Amniotic fluid embolism with consumptive coagulopathy
A cervical laceration sustained during the second stage of labor
Uterine inversion requiring immediate manual replacement
Placenta accreta spectrum
questions.exp: Prior cesarean plus previa is the classic setup for placenta accreta spectrum, and a retained, non-separating placenta with hemorrhage is accreta until proven otherwise; avoid forceful traction and prepare for surgery with early multidisciplinary planning.
why: Endometritis and retained products cause late bleeding days to weeks after birth, not at delivery.
A consumptive coagulopathy would not explain a placenta that refuses to separate from the wall.
A laceration bleeds with a firm, well-contracted fundus and a placenta already delivered.
Uterine inversion presents with a fundus that cannot be palpated abdominally, not a placenta that will not separate.

questions.q: A woman returns 12 days after delivery with heavy bleeding and foul-smelling lochia. How is this best characterized and evaluated?
ch: Normal lochia; reassure the patient and discharge without evaluation
Uterine atony; the 24-hour rule does not apply to bleeding this heavy
Secondary PPH from retained products or endometritis; evaluate with ultrasound and antibiotics
Thrombin-type hemorrhage; transfuse cryoprecipitate empirically
Primary postpartum hemorrhage; give oxytocin and observe her
questions.exp: Secondary or late PPH occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum and is more often retained products or endometritis with subinvolution, warranting ultrasound with or without antibiotics; foul-smelling lochia is exactly what postpartum patients are taught to report.
why: Foul-smelling lochia with heavy bleeding is precisely what patients are taught to report as abnormal.
The timing distinction does apply, and atony is not the usual cause of bleeding this late.
Empiric cryoprecipitate treats coagulopathy, which is not the likely mechanism this far from delivery.
Primary PPH is defined as occurring within 24 hours of birth, so the timing does not fit.
